jhmt-2020-ms-short-01.title: Three constraints
jhmt-2020-ms-short-01.body: If Sungwon has $x$ dollars, ordering at most 3 salmon means $\lfloor x/12.95 \rfloor = 3$, i.e.~$38.85 \le x < 51.80$. At most 5 chicken gives $43.75 \le x < 52.50$. At most 6 tuna gives $49.50 \le x < 57.75$. The intersection is $49.50 \le x < 51.80$. The largest whole number in this range is $\boxed{51}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-04.title: Case analysis
jhmt-2020-ms-short-04.body:
**Case 1: a corner is filled.** All four corners are equivalent under the symmetries, so say the top-left corner is filled. The second square can be any of the other $7$ squares, and these $7$ designs are all different (no symmetry other than the identity keeps the top-left corner fixed).

**Case 2: no corner is filled.** Then both filled squares are among the $4$ middle squares; say the left square of the second row is filled. The second square is one of the other $3$ middle squares, giving $3$ more designs.

Total: $7+3=\boxed{10}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-04.title: Burnside count
jhmt-2020-ms-short-04.body: The grid has four symmetries: the identity, the $180^\circ$ rotation, and the two reflections. The identity fixes all $\binom82=28$ choices. Each of the other three symmetries swaps the $8$ squares in $4$ pairs and fixes no square, so it fixes exactly the $4$ choices consisting of one swapped pair. By Burnside's lemma the number of designs is $\frac{28+4+4+4}{4}=\boxed{10}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-05.title: Perfect squares
jhmt-2020-ms-short-05.body: Switch $k$ is flipped by robot $j$ whenever $j$ divides $k$. It ends up on iff it is flipped an odd number of times, i.e.~iff $k$ has an odd number of divisors. A positive integer has an odd number of divisors if and only if it is a perfect square. The perfect squares from 1 to 40 are $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36$ — that is $\boxed{6}$ switches.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-06.title: Height and Pythagorean theorem
jhmt-2020-ms-short-06.body: Height: $h = \frac{2 \times 600}{18+32} = 24$. Since $O$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, we have $PO = OQ = 12$. By symmetry $AO = 15$ and $DO = 20$ (applying the Pythagorean theorem: $AO^2 = 9^2 + 12^2 = 225$, $DO^2 = 16^2 + 12^2 = 400$). Draw $AX \perp DC$; the leg $DX = (32-18)/2 = 7$, so $DA = \sqrt{7^2+24^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$. Perimeter $= AO + DO + DA = 15+20+25 = \boxed{60}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-07.title: Radius chain
jhmt-2020-ms-short-07.body: $4\pi r_A^2 = 16\pi \Rightarrow r_A = 2$. The cube has side $2r_A = 4$. The hemisphere's radius equals the hypotenuse from the center of the base to a top corner: $r_C^2 = 4^2 + (2\sqrt{2})^2 = 16+8 = 24$, so $r_C = \sqrt{24}$. Surface area of hemisphere: curved part $= \frac{4\pi r_C^2}{2} = 2\pi(24) = 48\pi$; flat circle $= \pi r_C^2 = 24\pi$. Total $= 72\pi$, so $k = \boxed{72}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-08.title: Radius from diagonal constraint
jhmt-2020-ms-short-08.body: Each circle of radius $r$ has its center at distance $r\sqrt{2}$ from the nearest corner. The two centers are $2r$ apart (externally tangent), and the total distance from corner to corner along the diagonal is $12\sqrt{2}$. So $2r\sqrt{2} + 2r = 12\sqrt{2}$, giving $r = \frac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}+1} = \frac{6\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}-1)}{1} = 12 - 6\sqrt{2}$. Thus $a=12$, $b=6$, $c=2$, and $a+b+c = \boxed{20}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-09.title: Stars and bars
jhmt-2020-ms-short-09.body: Count non-negative integer solutions to $a+b+c = 7$. By stars and bars: $\dbinom{7+3-1}{3-1} = \dbinom{9}{2} = \boxed{36}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-10.title: Substitute and minimize
jhmt-2020-ms-short-10.body: With $y = 5-x$: $f(x) + g(5-x) = x^2+2x + 3(5-x)-14 = x^2 - x + 1$. This parabola has vertex at $x = \frac{1}{2}$, so the minimum stress occurs when Elvin studies $\frac{1}{2}$ hour and does chores for $y = 5-\frac{1}{2} = \frac{9}{2}$ hours. Thus $a+b = 9+2 = \boxed{11}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-11.title: Derangement product
jhmt-2020-ms-short-11.body: The prime digits $\{2,3,5,7\}$ occupy positions 2, 3, 5, 7 and must stay among those positions (a derangement of 4 objects: $D_4 = 9$). The non-prime digits $\{1,4,6,8,9\}$ occupy positions 1, 4, 6, 8, 9 and must derange among themselves ($D_5 = 44$). Total fresh numbers: $D_4 \times D_5 = 9 \times 44 = \boxed{396}$.

jhmt-2020-ms-short-12.title: Similar triangles and incircles
jhmt-2020-ms-short-12.body:
Let the square have side $k$. Since $XY\parallel AB$, $\triangle CXY\sim\triangle CAB$, so $\frac{CX}{XY}=\frac{CA}{AB}$, i.e. $\frac{6-k}{k}=\frac{6}{12}$, giving $k=4$. Thus $CX=2$, $XY=4$, $ZY=4$, $ZB=8$.

The hypotenuse of $\triangle ABC$ is $\sqrt{6^2+12^2}=6\sqrt5$, and its inradius is $\frac{6+12-6\sqrt5}{2}=9-3\sqrt5$. Triangles $CXY$ (legs $2,4$) and $ZYB$ (legs $4,8$) are similar to $\triangle CAB$ with ratios $\frac13$ and $\frac23$, so their inradii are $r=3-\sqrt5$ and $R=6-2\sqrt5$.

Place $A=(0,0)$, $B=(12,0)$, $C=(0,6)$, so $X=(0,4)$, $Y=(4,4)$, $Z=(4,0)$. The incenter of a right triangle is at distance equal to its inradius from both legs. In $\triangle CXY$ (right angle at $X$) the legs lie on $x=0$ and $y=4$, so $P=(r,4+r)$. In $\triangle ZYB$ (right angle at $Z$) the legs lie on $x=4$ and $y=0$, so $Q=(4+R,R)$. Hence
$$PQ^2=(4+R-r)^2+(4+r-R)^2=(7-\sqrt5)^2+(1+\sqrt5)^2=(54-14\sqrt5)+(6+2\sqrt5)=60-12\sqrt5.$$
So $f+g+j=60+12+5=\boxed{77}$.
